title: “HUSBAND OF ONE WIFE”: THE FOUR WORDS THAT COULD EXPOSE WHAT WE’VE BEEN GETTING WRONG ABOUT CHURCH LEADERSHIP
paragraphs: “HUSBAND OF ONE WIFE”: THE FOUR WORDS THAT COULD EXPOSE WHAT WE’VE BEEN GETTING WRONG ABOUT CHURCH LEADERSHIP

Does God simply require a pastor to have one wife—or is He demanding something far deeper: a life of covenant faithfulness, sexual integrity, and Christlike character that cannot be manufactured behind a pulpit?
There is something deeply unsettling about a man who can preach beautifully about faithfulness while quietly betraying the people who trust him.
He can quote Scripture with tears in his eyes.
He can speak about holiness with conviction in his voice.
He can stand before hundreds of people, lift his Bible, and declare that marriage is sacred.
And yet, when the microphone is turned off, when the congregation has gone home, when nobody is watching...
Who is he really?
That question is uncomfortable.
But perhaps it is exactly the question the apostle Paul wanted the Church to ask.
Because tucked inside Paul's instructions about church leadership is a phrase that has sparked centuries of discussion, disagreement, and sometimes painful misunderstanding.
“The husband of one wife.”
Four words in familiar English translations.
Simple enough to memorize.
Complicated enough to divide churches.
Some insist these words mean a pastor must never have more than one wife at a time.
Others argue that a man who has ever been divorced and remarried is permanently disqualified from ministry.
Still others believe Paul was primarily describing a man whose heart, conduct, and relationships demonstrate unwavering marital faithfulness.
And then comes a question many congregations rarely consider:
What if we have spent so much time counting a leader's marriages that we have forgotten to examine his character?
That does not mean marital history is irrelevant.
It means we must be careful not to make Paul's words say less—or more—than Scripture actually teaches.
Because this passage is not merely about who is allowed to stand behind a pulpit.
It is about the kind of person who can be trusted to care for the people Jesus purchased with His own blood.
And when we examine the original Greek, the surrounding passages, and the heart of the Gospel, something powerful begins to emerge.
Something that should humble every pastor.
Challenge every church.
And remind every wounded believer that Jesus Christ is not interested in religious appearances.
He is interested in truth.
Paul writes:
—1 Timothy 3:1–2, King James Version
Now look closely at the Greek expression behind the familiar English words.
μιᾶς γυναικὸς ἄνδρα
Transliteration: mias gynaikos andra.
A close, literal rendering is:
“A man of one woman,” or “a one-woman man.”
The Greek word mias means “one,” gynaikos is the genitive form of a word that can mean “woman” or “wife,” and andra is a form of the word for “man” or “husband.”
Because the words for man and woman can also mean husband and wife in the appropriate context, the traditional translation “husband of one wife” is entirely legitimate.
But the wording raises an important interpretive question.
Was Paul merely specifying the number of wives a leader could have?
Or was he describing the kind of man a leader must be?
To understand that, we cannot isolate one phrase and ignore everything around it.
We must allow Scripture to speak in context.
And the context is revealing.
Paul does not begin by asking whether a man is charismatic.
He does not ask whether he has a large following.
He does not ask whether his sermons receive thousands of views.
He does not ask whether his church owns an impressive building.
He begins with something far more difficult to imitate.
Character.
The overseer must be above reproach.
Self-controlled.
Respectable.
Hospitable.
Able to teach.
Not addicted to wine.
Not violent.
Not greedy.
Not quarrelsome.
Able to manage his household well.
And respected even by outsiders.
Read that again.
Paul is describing a recognizable pattern of life, not merely a collection of religious credentials.
A man may be legally married to one woman and still be unfaithful to her.
He may have only one wife and still cultivate secret sexual relationships.
He may never have divorced and still treat his wife with cruelty.
He may publicly defend biblical marriage while privately humiliating the woman he promised to love.
Would satisfying a numerical requirement somehow make such a man spiritually qualified?
Of course not.
That is why the expression “a one-woman man” has led many biblical interpreters to emphasize marital fidelity and sexual integrity.
A leader's covenant commitments should not be contradicted by his hidden conduct.
His private life should not expose his public preaching as a performance.
A wedding ring is not proof of faithfulness. A marriage certificate is not proof of godliness. And a microphone is certainly not proof of spiritual maturity.
But we must be equally careful here.
The phrase does not give us permission to dismiss the number of spouses as unimportant.
In its historical setting, the language naturally excludes a man who has multiple wives simultaneously. It also fits Paul's broader expectation of marital fidelity.
The question is whether it excludes only polygamy or carries additional implications concerning sexual conduct, divorce, remarriage, and the public reputation of a church leader.
Christians who take Scripture seriously have disagreed about some of those implications.
And faithful interpretation requires us to acknowledge where the text is clear and where difficult questions remain.
The same Greek expression appears again in Titus 1:6, where Paul describes an elder as:
“If any be blameless, the husband of one wife, having faithful children not accused of riot or unruly.”
—Titus 1:6, KJV
Again, the qualification appears within a larger description of a leader's household and character.
That matters.
Paul is not conducting a marriage census.
He is establishing standards for those entrusted with spiritual oversight.
The Church must not treat leadership as a reward for popularity when Scripture treats it as a responsibility requiring tested character.
And there is another passage that makes the discussion even more interesting.
In 1 Timothy 5:9, Paul describes a widow who may be enrolled for church support, saying that she should have been:
“...the wife of one man.”
The corresponding Greek expression is:
ἑνὸς ἀνδρὸς γυνή
Transliteration: henos andros gynē.
Literally, “a woman of one man,” or, in context, “the wife of one husband.”
Notice the parallel.
For male overseers, Paul uses language that can be rendered “a one-woman man.”
For certain widows, he uses language that can be rendered “a one-man woman.”
This parallel strengthens the argument that fidelity and marital reputation are central concerns.
However, it does not settle every interpretive question.
Some interpreters understand the widow's qualification as referring to having been married only once. Others understand it as describing marital faithfulness.
That disagreement shows why we should avoid pretending that one English slogan resolves every possible situation.
Yet the moral direction of Paul's teaching is unmistakable.
Faithfulness matters to God.
Not only faithfulness when people are watching.
Not only faithfulness when temptation is absent.
Not only faithfulness when marriage feels easy.
Faithfulness when sacrifice is required.
Faithfulness when attention comes from someone who is not your spouse.
Faithfulness when nobody would immediately discover the compromise.
And faithfulness to the truth when maintaining a religious image would be more convenient.
Now consider the question of monogamy itself.
Was Paul requiring church leaders to practice monogamy?
The text certainly supports that expectation.
But biblical monogamy is not simply a rule invented by Paul for church administrators.
Its theological foundation reaches back to creation.
Genesis 2:24 declares:
“Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.”
The Hebrew phrase translated “one flesh” is:
בָּשָׂר אֶחָד
Transliteration: basar echad.
It means “one flesh.”
This is covenantal language describing the profound union of husband and wife.
The passage presents a man joined to his wife in a new family bond.
It is not merely a statement about physical intimacy.
It describes a relationship of belonging, commitment, and shared life.
And when Jesus was questioned about divorce, He did something extraordinary.
He directed His listeners back to creation.
In Matthew 19:4–6, Jesus referred to God creating humanity male and female, then cited the marriage union of Genesis and declared:
“What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.”
Jesus grounded His teaching in God's original design.
That matters because Scripture does contain accounts of men who had multiple wives.
Abraham.
Jacob.
David.
Solomon.
But we must never confuse biblical description with biblical approval.
The Bible sometimes records human behavior precisely so we can see its consequences.
And the consequences of polygamy in many Old Testament narratives are heartbreaking.
Rivalry.
Jealousy.
Family division.
Pain between children.
Competing loyalties.
Spiritual compromise.
Solomon's many wives, for example, became part of the tragedy described in 1 Kings 11, when his heart was turned toward other gods.
The existence of polygamy in biblical history does not establish it as God's ideal for Christian marriage.
Indeed, the creation pattern affirmed by Jesus and the New Testament's teaching on marital fidelity provide the theological foundation for the Church's historic commitment to monogamy.
So yes, “husband of one wife” is entirely consistent with requiring monogamy of church overseers.
But stopping there risks missing Paul's larger concern.
A man can reject polygamy and still betray the covenant of marriage.
That is the uncomfortable truth.
Imagine a pastor who has been married to the same woman for twenty-five years.
Every Sunday, they sit together.
They smile for photographs.
Their anniversary posts receive hundreds of congratulations.
Their marriage appears to be a beautiful testimony.
But at home, she is afraid to speak.
He controls her through intimidation.
He uses Scripture to silence her concerns.
He tells her that questioning his conduct means questioning God's authority.
He has never taken another wife.
But is he living as the faithful, gentle, self-controlled leader Paul describes?
No.
His conduct contradicts the surrounding qualifications.
And this is where churches must become courageous.
Because sometimes the greatest threat to a congregation is not a man who openly rejects biblical standards.
It is a man who knows how to quote those standards while hiding his violations of them.
Jesus warned about religious hypocrisy.
He spoke against those who appeared righteous outwardly while concealing corruption within.
And His warnings were not directed only at people outside the religious community.
They were directed at people who claimed to represent God.
This should make every spiritual leader tremble—not in hopeless terror, but in reverent accountability.
Because the sheep do not belong to the shepherd.
They belong to Christ.
Peter instructed elders not to dominate those entrusted to their care, but to become examples to the flock (1 Peter 5:2–3).
And Jesus Himself said:
“I am the good shepherd: the good shepherd giveth his life for the sheep.”
—John 10:11, KJV
That is the standard.
Not celebrity.
Not control.
Not unquestioned authority.
Sacrificial love.
A pastor is not called to build a personal kingdom.
He is called to serve the King who laid down His life.
But now we must enter one of the most sensitive parts of this discussion.
What about divorce?
What about remarriage?
What about a man whose first marriage ended in tragedy, betrayal, abandonment, or serious sin?
Does “husband of one wife” automatically disqualify him forever?
This is where careless certainty can wound people.
Some Christian traditions interpret Paul's words as requiring a church leader to have been married only once, with varying applications to widowhood and remarriage.
Others understand the phrase primarily as a requirement of present marital fidelity, while examining the circumstances of any divorce or remarriage in light of the rest of Scripture.
Still others distinguish between different biblical grounds for divorce and remarriage.
These differences are not trivial.
Marriage is sacred.
Divorce is serious.
Sexual sin is serious.
And the qualifications for spiritual leadership must never be treated casually.
Jesus addressed divorce and remarriage in Matthew 5:31–32 and Matthew 19:3–9.
Paul also addressed marital separation, reconciliation, and abandonment in 1 Corinthians 7.
Those passages must be considered together rather than forcing every situation into one isolated phrase.
A divorce caused by deliberate adultery is not morally identical to a divorce suffered by the betrayed spouse.
A person abandoned by an unbelieving partner has not necessarily committed the same wrong as someone who abandons a spouse to pursue another relationship.
And a widower who remarries after the death of his wife is not committing adultery simply by entering another marriage.
Romans 7:2–3 and 1 Corinthians 7:39 explicitly recognize that death ends the marital bond, leaving the surviving spouse free to remarry.
That alone should caution us against interpreting “one wife” as a simplistic lifetime numerical limit without considering the rest of Scripture.
But neither should we rush to the opposite extreme and declare that a leader's marital history never matters.
It can matter greatly.
Churches must carefully examine patterns of behavior, repentance, responsibility, reconciliation where appropriate, and the person's present reputation.
And even where forgiveness is genuine, suitability for church leadership remains a separate question.
Forgiveness is not the same thing as automatic restoration to office.
That distinction is essential.
A man may be forgiven by God and still need to step away from ministry.
A man may sincerely repent and still need to accept consequences.
A man may receive grace and still be required to rebuild trust over time.
And some forms of misconduct, especially abuse or exploitation, may make a return to spiritual authority inappropriate.
The Gospel never requires victims to surrender their safety so that a leader can recover his reputation.
Repentance does not erase the need for truth, protection, accountability, or justice.
That is not a rejection of grace.
It is part of taking righteousness seriously.
And perhaps someone reading this knows exactly why those words matter.
Perhaps you once trusted a pastor who failed you.
Perhaps you watched your family suffer because someone in spiritual authority refused correction.
Perhaps you were told to remain silent because speaking the truth might damage the church.
Perhaps you have carried questions for years.
Why did nobody notice?
Why did nobody intervene?
Why did people defend the leader more fiercely than they protected the wounded?
And maybe the deepest question was never about the pastor at all.
Maybe it was this:
“Jesus, if these people represented You, how can I trust You again?”
If that is your question, please hear something important.
The failures of people who claim Christ's name do not redefine the character of Christ Himself.
Jesus is not the hypocrisy that wounded you.
He is not the manipulation that silenced you.
He is not the betrayal that shattered your trust.
He is the righteous Shepherd who never uses His sheep for selfish gain.
He is the Savior who confronted religious hypocrisy.
He is the Lord who cares about the vulnerable.
He is the One who calls sinners to repentance and refuses to confuse outward appearances with inward righteousness.
And He does not ask you to call evil good.
You can acknowledge wrongdoing without abandoning truth.
You can seek healing without pretending the harm never happened.
You can forgive without restoring unsafe access or surrendering appropriate boundaries.
And you can return to Jesus without returning to the conditions that wounded you.
Because the Gospel is not a command to protect religious reputations.
It is the announcement that Jesus Christ came to save sinners and make people new.
That includes pastors.
That includes elders.
That includes husbands.
That includes wives.
That includes wounded believers.
And it includes the person reading this who has quietly realized that the problem is not only somewhere else.
Perhaps the Holy Spirit has brought something closer to home.
Maybe you have never been a pastor.
Maybe you have never stood behind a pulpit.
But you know what it means to present one version of yourself publicly while hiding another privately.
You know what it means to say the right things and still struggle with the wrong desires.
You know what it means to promise faithfulness while allowing compromise to grow in secret.
And perhaps you have been comforting yourself with a dangerous thought:
“At least nobody knows.”
But God knows.
Not because He delights in humiliating you.
Not because He is searching for an excuse to destroy you.
But because nothing hidden from human eyes is hidden from the Lord.
Hebrews 4:13 reminds us that all things are exposed before the One to whom we must give account.
And yet, only a few verses later, the same chapter invites believers to approach the throne of grace to receive mercy and find help in time of need (Hebrews 4:16).
Do you see the beauty of that?
The God who sees everything is also the God who invites repentant sinners to come to Him through Jesus Christ.
He does not offer permission to continue in darkness.
He offers mercy that calls us into the light.
The Greek word commonly translated “repentance” is μετάνοια, metanoia.
It refers to a change of mind or heart, understood in the New Testament as a turning toward God that bears fruit in a changed life.
Repentance is more than embarrassment at being discovered.
It is more than crying because consequences have arrived.
It is more than saying, “I'm sorry,” while protecting the behavior that caused the harm.
Genuine repentance turns from sin toward God.
It acknowledges wrongdoing.
It abandons excuses.
It accepts accountability.
And where possible and appropriate, it seeks to repair the harm done.
This is why the Gospel is so much greater than image management.
Religion without repentance may teach a person to conceal sin more effectively.
But grace received through faith in Christ teaches us to renounce ungodliness and live differently.
Titus 2:11–12 says:

“For the grace of God that bringeth salvation hath appeared to all men, Teaching us that, denying ungodliness and worldly lusts, we should live soberly, righteously, and godly, in this present world.”
Notice that grace does not merely comfort.
Grace teaches.
Grace transforms.
Grace calls us out of the very darkness from which Christ came to rescue us.
And that brings us back to the original question.
Does “husband of one wife” mean church leaders must be monogamous—or something more?

The most responsible answer is that Paul's language supports monogamy and calls for a reputation of marital faithfulness, but the surrounding qualifications show that his concern extends beyond marital status to the leader's entire character.
A faithful reading should not reduce the qualification to arithmetic.
Nor should it ignore the plain importance of exclusive marital commitment.
Paul is describing a man whose relationships and conduct are consistent with the sacred responsibility of spiritual oversight.
The phrase itself does not resolve every question about divorce, remarriage, widowhood, or whether an unmarried man may serve as an elder.
Those questions require careful consideration of the broader biblical witness.
Indeed, Paul himself was unmarried when he wrote about the advantages of singleness for undivided devotion to the Lord in 1 Corinthians 7.
Jesus was unmarried.
Neither Scripture nor the Greek expression should be casually used to suggest that unmarried Christians are spiritually inferior.
Churches differ over whether the qualification assumes marriage for elders or describes fidelity for those who are married.
What cannot be responsibly denied is that Christian leaders must exhibit holiness, integrity, self-control, and trustworthy conduct.
And all of this points beyond Paul.
Beyond church policies.
Beyond arguments about qualifications.
It points us to Jesus Christ.
The One who has never broken a covenant.
The One who has never deceived His people.
The One whose love is not a public performance.
The One who remained faithful even when faithfulness led Him to a cross.
Scripture describes Christ's relationship with His Church using the language of a bridegroom and bride.
Ephesians 5:25 declares:
“Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the church, and gave himself for it.”
That verse changes everything.
Because Christian marriage is not primarily a stage on which a man displays his authority.
It is a sacred relationship in which love should reflect the self-giving character of Christ.
And Christian leadership is not permission to demand sacrifices from everyone else while protecting oneself from accountability.
It is a calling to serve under the authority of the crucified and risen Lord.
Jesus gave Himself for His people.
He did not exploit them.
He did not abandon them.
He did not manipulate them.
He loved them sacrificially.
And the Church must never settle for leaders who publicly praise that love while privately rejecting its demands.
But here is where the story becomes personal for all of us.
Because none of us can stand before God claiming perfect righteousness through our own efforts.
Not the pastor.
Not the elder.
Not the husband who has been married for fifty years.
Not the believer who has never experienced divorce.
Not the person whose reputation appears spotless.
Romans 3:23 declares:
“For all have sinned, and come short of the glory of God.”
All.
That word leaves no room for spiritual superiority.
But it also prepares us for the extraordinary promise of the Gospel.
Jesus Christ lived the righteous life we could not live.
He died for our sins.
He rose again.
And everyone who turns to Him in repentance and faith can receive forgiveness and new life.
Second Corinthians 5:17 says:
“Therefore if any man be in Christ, he is a new creature: old things are passed away; behold, all things are become new.”
That is not a promise that every earthly consequence disappears.
It is not a guarantee that every broken relationship will be restored.
It is not permission to bypass the qualifications of church leadership.
It is something greater.
It is the promise that sin does not have to remain the master of the person who belongs to Jesus Christ.
Your past can be confessed.
Your heart can be transformed.
Your patterns can change.
Your future can be lived in obedience to the Savior who redeemed you.
And if you have failed, the answer is not to hide behind religious language.
Come into the light.
Confess what is true.
Seek the help and accountability you need.
Make no excuses for harm.
And trust the mercy of Christ enough to obey Him, even when obedience is costly.
Perhaps that is the most important lesson hidden inside this entire discussion.
God is not merely looking for leaders who can defend the biblical definition of faithfulness. He requires leaders who actually live faithfully.
And the rest of us are not exempt from the call to holiness simply because we do not hold church office.
The same Jesus who calls shepherds to integrity calls every believer to walk in truth.
The same Gospel that forgives sinners also transforms them.
The same grace that restores hope also confronts hypocrisy.
So before we ask whether someone else is qualified to lead, perhaps we should also ask:
Am I allowing Christ to rule the parts of my life nobody else sees?
Am I faithful in my commitments?
Am I honest about my struggles?
Have I confused religious activity with spiritual maturity?
And when the truth exposes something painful, will I run toward Jesus—or retreat further into hiding?
If this article has exposed a struggle you have been carrying, you do not have to publish the details of your private life to prove your sincerity.
Not because a comment earns God's forgiveness.
Not because public words can replace private repentance.
They cannot.
But because sometimes a simple expression of surrender encourages another struggling believer to seek Christ as well.
You may discover that others have been carrying similar wounds.
Please remember that sensitive disclosures, especially those involving abuse, deserve safe and confidential support rather than pressure to share publicly.
There is something else I want to ask you to consider.
Not merely because it contains Greek words or difficult theological questions.
And you may need to return to these truths.
Your profile may reach someone this page never reaches.
Someone who has quietly walked away from church.
Someone who thinks Christianity is nothing more than religious hypocrisy.
Someone whose marriage is struggling.
Someone who needs to understand that the failures of human shepherds do not erase the faithfulness of the Good Shepherd.
Not to embarrass them.
Not to accuse them.
Not to turn Scripture into a weapon.
But to invite them into a deeper understanding of God's Word.
Because biblical truth is not meant to become ammunition for humiliating people.
It is meant to lead us toward Christ.
We want to help believers open their Bibles, examine difficult questions, recognize deception, grow in discernment, experience the hope of the Gospel, and follow Jesus with greater faithfulness.
Those resources are intended to help believers who are serious about growing deeper in Jesus Christ.
And keeping resources freely accessible while continuing to create, maintain, and expand this work requires real time, labor, and financial support.
Not out of guilt.
You glorify God through faith in Christ, obedience to His Word, love for others, and faithful stewardship of what He has entrusted to you.
Supporting sound biblical teaching and discipleship can be one meaningful expression of that stewardship.
It can help us keep creating Scripture-centered articles, developing discipleship resources, and making biblical teaching available to people who may never be able to pay for it.
Second Corinthians 9:7 teaches that giving should not be reluctant or compelled, because God loves a cheerful giver.
If you have a local church, please continue to take seriously your responsibilities to your congregation and the needs of your family. We are not asking you to neglect those commitments.
We are simply inviting those who have been spiritually nourished by Gospel Warrior to prayerfully consider helping nourish others.
Those products can serve as reminders of biblical truth, conversation starters, or thoughtful gifts.
It is the opportunity to participate in making Christ-centered teaching and free discipleship resources more widely available.
Read.
Learn.
Pray.
Invite others.
Continue growing in the Word.
You do not have to pay to belong among those who seek Jesus.
But before you leave, I want to bring you back to the question that began this entire conversation.
Does “husband of one wife” mean a church leader must be monogamous—or something more?
It means we must take the biblical standard of marital faithfulness seriously.
It means we must examine the whole counsel of Scripture rather than reducing a complex qualification to a convenient slogan.
It means church leaders must not merely appear respectable but must demonstrate the character required of those entrusted with God's people.
And it reminds us that no human leader, however gifted, stands above accountability.
But there is one final truth I do not want you to miss.
The most faithful Shepherd in the history of the world never stood before a congregation asking people to admire His perfect marriage.
He stood before sinners and offered Himself.
Jesus Christ, the Bridegroom of the Church, loved His people all the way to the cross.
He bore sin.
He conquered death.
He rose in victory.
And He is coming again.
The hope of the Church has never been that every pastor will be flawless.
The hope of the Church is that Jesus Christ is faithful even when human beings fail.
That truth does not excuse unfaithfulness.
It gives us a reason to repent.
It gives the wounded a reason to hope.
It gives leaders a reason to walk humbly.
And it gives sinners a Savior worth trusting.
So when you hear the words “husband of one wife” again, remember that the issue is not simply what a man can claim about his marital status.
The issue is whether his life reflects the truth he has been entrusted to proclaim.
And beyond every imperfect earthly shepherd stands the One who will never betray His flock.
Perhaps your story has been marked by scandal.
Perhaps by broken promises.
Perhaps by betrayal.
Perhaps by sins you deeply regret.
But if you belong to Jesus Christ, your darkest chapter does not have to become your final chapter.
Bring the truth into His light.
Receive His mercy through repentance and faith.
Walk in obedience.
And let the Gospel—not your shame, not your reputation, not the failures of others—have the final word.
The hands that were pierced for your redemption will never use your wounds to hide someone else's sin.
